steps.content: The creaking of a door...
With a creak that makes one's teeth tingle, Raven pushes open the door to the study.
You find yourself in a room jammed full of photos, clippings, magazines, so numerous that they fill up at least a dozen shelves of varying sizes.
This room is one-quarter the size of the MBCC's archive room.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Are these...
You take a notebook from one of the shelves, shake off the dust, and open it.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: These are all records about the history of Syndicate, from N.F. 81 to N.F. 114, some by me, some by others.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I've tried my best to collect the epic tales of every Syndican hero; I don't want any of their stories to be buried and never see the day of light.

options: When did you start collecting them?

choices.text: When did you start collecting them?

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Some time after I arrived in Eastside, I guess. My family moved to Eastside when I was a child.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: That explains why you look sad in some of your childhood photos.
The few photos of a gloomy young Raven stand out on the photo wall.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Yeah, Eastside is just for show; it's actually quite boring.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: The boredom wasn't relieved until, on TV, I saw how those heroes stepped up in times of crisis; they were like a fire in the dark.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: That's when I found the goal I wished to pursue.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Ever since then, I had been jotting things down as a hobby. And just like that, more than a decade passed.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Maybe because life in Eastside was too boring for me, or maybe because I wanted to visit my childhood hometown...

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I ended up becoming a writer for Yagyu's newspaper; I wrote articles for their official account.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Hahaha... The funny thing is, while I was working in that place, I realized that no one could match me when it came to sensationalism and writing eye-catching news.
Raven holds up a finger, words pouring out of her mouth as she excitedly recounts her glorious past.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: One year later, in N.F. 103, the newspaper sent me to Syndicate. But it wasn't the Syndicate I remembered from my childhood.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Ruins were everywhere, war was widespread, devastation as far as the eye could see...

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: It was then that I saw that fire in the dark.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Yes. You're quick on the uptake, aren't you? Anyway, I became an embedded reporter, living off them... no, I mean, reporting on their activities.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: It was a troubled period. The relationship between the miners and Nirvana was extremely tense; Nirvana planned to do away with the mining machines, and the miners wouldn't hear of it.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: The miners fought back. They went all out, eventually stopping that arrogant Nirvana from going through with their plan, at least temporarily, and forcing them to the negotiation table.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Of course, I wasn't idle either. I put up banners for them, wrote slogans, and even helped them drag back a couple of machines.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: That's a great story, right?
You nod.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: That's not the end of it, though.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Ah, the hero defeats the villain, and the faint light turns into a blazing fire, illuminating the inky night.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: But even the fiercest fire is no match for torrential rain. That's exactly what happened to our heroes. After the W-31 incident, a Black Ring appeared, and the leadership of the organization disappeared in mysterious circumstances.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: After I returned to Eastside, I tried hard to publicize their heroic deeds, hoping that they could be remembered.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: However, as you must have known, in Eastside at that time, articles about Nirvana would be removed from circulation as soon as they were published.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: They would invite the writers for "coffee," to give them some "friendly advice."

options: How many times were you invited?

choices.text: How many times were you invited?

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Well, let me put it this way... More times than I'd been home. I could walk around the Eastside Public Security Bureau's office with my eyes closed.
Raven shrugs, a nonchalant look on her face.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: The heroic deeds I recorded posed a threat to them. Sure enough, they soon made their move against me.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I became a target for DRD, Nirvana's special department, because I knew too much about the W-31 incident. They pinned such charges as "endangering Eastside's public security," "repeatedly disrupting public order," "spreading false information" on me.

options: What did they do to you?

choices.text: What did they do to you?

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I was fine. Just a few scratches here and there. They were nothing; they couldn't break me, not at all.
Raven dismisses your concern with a wave of her hand. She looks relaxed, describing her ordeal like it's no big deal.
But it couldn't have been easy on her. Nirvana's secret department would never let their enemies go with only a slap on their wrist.
Do you confess?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Haha, writing about the honorable deeds of heroes is a crime in your eyes, huh?
Your brain isn't working well, it seems. You guys, teach her a lesson about how to make a proper confession.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Ah, do your worst. It'll only strengthen the case that those people are heroes!
Take her away. Give her some alone time to think things over.
Do you confess?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: I've recorded... their heroic deeds...
Oh my, I've never seen anyone so foolish.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Haha, hahaha...
Why are you laughing? Have you gone mad?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Yes... I record stories of heroes...

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: In those stories... dirty rats like you... play a part too. You're there to make the heroes appear even more noble by comparison...
Crazy woman.
Beat her to within an inch of her life, but don't let her die.
Do you confess?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: ...Hahaha, you're afraid of the heroes of Syndicate... afraid that you're going to be burned by Rustfire...
You still have the strength to yell? With your broken ribs and all.
Lock her up. I've had enough of this crazy woman.
The ordeal doesn't seem to have broken her spirit. She is a true fighter.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Have you found something interesting in the notebook?
When Raven draws closer to take a peak, you quickly turn to the next page.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Just some records. What gave you the idea of becoming a teacher, anyway? You don't strike me as the kind of person who might be interested in teaching.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: You have a point there. If DRD had let up a bit on their effort to make my life miserable, maybe I wouldn't have thought of becoming a teacher.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: They couldn't do anything about me, so they sent me to a detention center on the border between Eastside and Syndicate.

options: The conditions there must have been appalling.

choices.text: The conditions there must have been appalling.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: They were. But that's only half of it. The worst part about the whole experience was that I got no one to talk to. Even the person who delivered my meals wouldn't get near me.
She had it tough. She had to endure the appalling conditions while still recovering from serious injuries.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Here is the thing about not having anyone to talk to. It prevents me from sharing my beautiful poems with other people.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: If I can't share them, how is the name of Raven, the Great Poet of DisCity, supposed to spread throughout the world?!
Raven bangs on the table, and dust falls from the shelves around you.
Typical Raven.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: There was one saving grace, though. The window was not very high. I could reach it if I put something under my feet.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Through the window, I always saw this group of Syndican kids giving the guards hell.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: They mocked these guards, every day without fail, or threw rocks and made faces at them.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Haha... it was quite satisfying. Because of the West District Treaty, all the guards could do was chase them away, angry as they were. Even at their angriest, they only dared to fire shots skyward.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: So, every day, I'd sit on the window ledge, cheering the kids on, waving at them.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: ...I don't know when exactly, but one day, one of the kids appeared on the other side of the iron bars.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: What's your name?

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Miles, and yours?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Raye.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: How long have you been locked up here, Raye?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Over a month now. They brought me in because I spread stories of heroes.
I cast a glance at the wall covered with the horizontal and vertical lines I had carved. And I saw my opportunity.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Hehe... Can you do me a favor? Just a small one.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: No.
Tsk tsk, the kid was sharp.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Hahaha... Come on, I just need you to get some notes out of this place for me. It's an easy task.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: No.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Not even if the notes are actually poems written by the most famous poet in all of Syndicate? This is a once-in-lifetime opportunity for you to earn a place in the history books.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: No.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Seriously? What's the matter? Don't tell me that you've lived in Syndicate all this time and never heard of my nickname name—Raven?

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: No.
The kid on the other side of the bars shakes his head.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: And... I don't want to be a Syndican; I want to go to Eastside.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Ah, what's so good about that rotten place? The lights at night can blind you!

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: At least I won't starve over there.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: ...But my friends told me that if you want to survive in Eastside, you'll have to know how to write.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Lucky for you, you've come to the right person. Miles, I want to apologize, because I've kept a big secret from you.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Well, actually...

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Actually what?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Actually, I'm a teacher.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: What's a teacher?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: You don't know? A teacher is someone who passes on knowledge, teaches you how to write. A teacher sometimes teaches a poem or two to the students too.
I emphasized the word "write." When he heard it, his eyes brightened and started seeing me in a different light.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Did you get today's poem out yet?

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Yeah, I posted it on their front door when the guards weren't watching.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Bravo! I knew I picked the right person! Now, let's start our lesson.
I struck a deal with this Miles kid. I taught him to write, disguised as a teacher, and he helped me get my poems out of this closed-off detention center.
This is how the lesson went: I taught him the pronunciations of a few words, and then I wrote them down on a piece of paper and passed the paper and pen out of the window.
On that memorable day, Miles didn't start writing right away when I passed him the paper and pen.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: What's the matter? Are today's words too difficult for you?

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: It's not that... Um, can you finish Heroes of Syndicate first?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Cough... cough...
That was something I came up with on the spot the day before, to get him to help get my poems out. As a good "teacher," how could I say no to a student's request?

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: Sure thing. Let's pick up where we left off yesterday. Remind me where we were yesterday.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Julien the Fate Challenger!

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: All right, let's talk about another hero of Rustfire then. This one is called the Thunder Halberd!

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Wow, that name sounds badass...

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Miss Raye...

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: What's the matter?
Miles was practicing writing on the other side of the window. Although his handwriting was still crooked and oftentimes illegible, it was much better than when he first started.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: I think Syndicate isn't so bad after all. I want to stay.

steps.speaker: Raye
steps.content: You don't want to go to Eastside anymore?

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: No, I don't. I used to despise Syndicate, thought it was a decrepit place.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: I don't think so now, after hearing you tell me about what it has been through, what it used to look like, and how countless people have fought on its behalf.

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: Plus...

steps.speaker: Miles
steps.content: It would be selfish of me to think only of filling my own belly. I want all my friends to have enough to eat.
I looked out of the window at Miles, who was absorbed in copying out my poetry.
I knew those were just the words of an innocent kid, but I saw the fire of resolve in his eyes when he said them.
I couldn't help but think, "If only I were a real teacher. Then I could teach him even more things, better things."
"If everything went right, maybe he could one day become a poet and write poems for me."
And then something went wrong. It hit when I least expected it. Somehow, my poetry was discovered by the guards of the detention center.
I was stripped of what few privileges I had been allowed. They took away my pen, ink, paper... They also kept Miles from making contact with me.
If they thought that was enough to shut me up, they had another thing coming.
I kept on writing. Since I had no way of getting my writings out of that place anymore, l left them where they were.
I looked for brick, plaster, anything with color in it, and turned it into my pen.
When I used up these items, when I couldn't scrape any bit of plaster from the walls of my cell...
I bit my own fingertip bloody and continued writing the heroic tales of Syndicate with my blood.
I wanted those heroes to be remembered, I wanted them to serve as an inspiration for future generations; I wrote for Miles, and for myself.
My body grew weak with each passing day due to oxygen deprivation and blood loss. My eyesight was failing fast.
Even the words I wrote down were crooked. They looked like crows in my failing eyesight. The whole thing was absurd...
Right before I closed my eyes and lost consciousness, I saw the words on the wall spout wings and fly out through the gaps between the iron bars one by one.
When I regained consciousness, I found that the words on the wall were gone, and there were crows in the cell. They were circling around a piece of paper on the floor, cawing.
They seemed to know I was awake; one of them picked up the piece of paper in its beak and flew over to drop it in my hand.
I opened the note. On it was the crooked handwriting that I had grown so familiar with...
"Thank you, Miss Raye."
They thought they could stop me from writing poetry; it's laughable.
My will was a crow that had long since flown out of her cage.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: That's how you became a Sinner, and that's also when you decided to become a teacher.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: That's right. From that point on, the prison staff could do nothing about me. That's when Raye stopped talking, and Raven started speaking.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: With no evidence whatsoever against me, they had to let me go.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: After my release, I put my newfound power to good use. To get back at those bastards, I went to a lot of trouble in Syndicate and Eastside. Of course, my power grew stronger with each of my life-and-death adventures.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I saw Donald, who was treated as a traitor back then, in that psychiatric hospital. He begged me not to tell Julien that he was alive, but I ignored his plea.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Soon afterward, I joined Rustfire and became a capable member of the organization. That gave me a chance to witness the changes in Syndicate.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Oh by the way, I also tracked down the DRD members who had tortured me and gave them a good beating.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: After that, you joined the Executive Committee as an undercover agent, right?

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Yes. And the next part of my story is about my encounters with you and your MBCC.
Epic stories of heroes, great individuals who worked tirelessly to change Syndicate for the better, battles against oppression...
These must be the kind of history that Raven wants to record.
You walk over to Raven's desk and pick up the textbook with the word "History" written on the cover. This is the revised textbook that she has been working on.
You open it, expecting to be awed by the poet's masterpiece.
But you don't find what you expected.
With the exception of the first page, where the events that transpired in Syndicate in N.F. 81 are recorded, the rest are blank.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: Why is it mostly blank? You changed your mind about telling the stories of Syndicate to your students?
Raven opens her mouth, but nothing comes out.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I didn't.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I told the stories of Syndicate to someone before.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I told him about the hypocrisy of Eastside, the craftiness of Nirvana, the injustice of the W-31 incident; I gave him hope with stories about heroes.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: He died.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Miles died.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: He hated Eastside, hated Nirvana, hated all enemies of Syndicate.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: In a foolhardy act, he stole a weapon from a Rustfire soldier, jumped over a fence, and got shot in the head by a bullet.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: It was my fault. If I hadn't filled his head with all those stories and ideals, he would've stayed in Rustfire as my first student.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: ...I remember clearly that that was the only time I ever got angry with Julien; I blamed him for the failure to keep the kid safe.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: But I was not only angry at him; I was angry at myself too.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Children have a right to the truth, but the truth can be too heavy for them to bear.
Raven hands you her wrinkled press pass.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: In Syndicate, there are already too many kids like that; they act on what their guts tell them.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Ica wants to avenge his parents' death, because they were captured by the executive officers and died in a detention center.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: Crache hates all adults indiscriminately, because she was sold to Yagyu.

steps.speaker: Raven
steps.content: I still love the stories of heroes who fought the dark forces, but what kind of stories should I pass on to these children?
You step forward and hold Raven's trembling hands.

steps.speaker: Chief
steps.content: But I hope that in tomorrow's class, you'll give the children another chance to choose.
